34-1.title: Before taking two cold or pain relievers at once, compare the ingredient lists: only one of them should contain paracetamol
34-1.inPlainWords: Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, is in most multi-symptom cold and flu products, in many headache and dental pain tablets, and in some prescription painkillers. Two such products taken together are one double dose, and a paracetamol overdose destroys the liver: in the U.S. study below, 27 per cent of the patients with paracetamol-related acute liver failure died before a transplant could be found. Read the panel that says 'each tablet contains' or 'each 5 ml contains' on every pack, and add up the paracetamol. An Indian adult pack usually caps the day at 4,000 mg, with a lower limit for anyone with liver disease, heavy alcohol use or a very low body weight, and the line printed on your own pack governs.
34-1.benefit: Over six years, 22 U.S. hospitals tracked 662 cases of acute liver failure. Of these, 275 (42 per cent) were caused by paracetamol; the median amount taken was 24 grams. Among those 275 patients, 131 (48 per cent) took the drug unintentionally, and in 38 per cent of those cases they were also taking two or more other paracetamol-containing products. In the end 27 per cent died before a transplant was possible and 8 per cent received one. U.S. rules require an over-the-counter pack to name three risks in the liver warning: exceeding the daily limit, using another paracetamol product at the same time, and drinking more than three alcoholic drinks a day while taking it. The Indian labelling rules in the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 require every active ingredient and its quantity to be printed on the pack, so the number you need is on the box.
34-1.cost: No cost at all. It takes a minute or two to read the ingredient panel on each pack you already own.
34-1.caveats: Do not add a paracetamol-containing cold medicine to a paracetamol tablet, and check combination painkillers sold for dental, back or period pain, plus prescription products such as tramadol with paracetamol, which count too. Do not drink heavily while taking it. Brand names hide the ingredient, so look for 'paracetamol' or 'acetaminophen' in the panel, not at the front of the box. If you think you have taken too much, go to a hospital now even if you feel well, because the antidote works best within the first eight hours and an overdose can feel like nothing at all. The evidence grade is B because the U.S. figures come from a registry without a control group.
34-1.sources: Larson AM, Polson J, Fontana RJ, et al.; Acute Liver Failure Study Group (2005). Acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure: results of a United States multicenter, prospective study. Hepatology, 42(6):1364-1372. <https://doi.org/10.1002/hep.20948>; 21 CFR 201.326, over-the-counter internal analgesic, antipyretic and antirheumatic drug products for over-the-counter human use. <https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-201/subpart-G/section-201.326>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/opencms/en/Home/>

34-2.title: Never give a child aspirin for a fever, and treat nimesulide or metamizole as an adult's drug, not a child's
34-2.inPlainWords: For a child's fever the two ordinary choices are paracetamol or ibuprofen, dosed by body weight, and nothing else. Aspirin given to a child during a viral illness can trigger Reye's syndrome, a rare swelling of the brain and liver that killed roughly a third of the children it struck before the warnings went out, which is why no child should get aspirin for a fever. Nimesulide is not a first-line medicine for a child and has been restricted in many countries over liver injury, and metamizole, sold as dipyrone or analgin, can cause a sudden dangerous fall in white blood cells and is not a standard children's medicine anywhere. The trap is a branded cold or pain tablet that hides one of these in its ingredient panel.
34-2.benefit: Reye's syndrome follows a viral illness, usually influenza or chickenpox, and causes brain swelling with fatty liver. U.S. surveillance from 1981 to 1997 recorded 1,207 cases in children under 18, and 82 per cent of them had salicylates, the aspirin family, detectable in the blood. The overall mortality was 31 per cent. Cases peaked at 555 in 1980, the year warnings began, and stayed under 36 a year from 1987 onwards. A parent in India is unlikely to be offered aspirin for a fever, but it is still in some adult headache tablets and in a few combination products, so the ingredient panel is worth the ten seconds.
34-2.cost: No cost: you simply check the generic name before you buy, and a strip of paediatric paracetamol is inexpensive.
34-2.caveats: Look for 'acetylsalicylic acid' or 'aspirin' in the panel rather than trusting the front of the packet. Do not break an adult tablet in half for a child; the dose is set by weight, and a pharmacist will work it out. An infant under three months with any fever goes to hospital the same day. A dehydrated or vomiting child should not be given ibuprofen, because it is harder on the kidneys. The evidence grade is B: the Reye's figures come from surveillance, not a controlled trial, though the fall in cases after the warnings is hard to explain any other way.
34-2.sources: Belay ED, Bresee JS, Holman RC, Khan AS, Shahriari A, Schonberger LB (1999). Reye's syndrome in the United States from 1981 through 1997. New England Journal of Medicine, 340(18):1377-1382. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199905063401801>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/opencms/en/Home/>

34-4.title: Do not give a child under two an over-the-counter cold or cough medicine on your own
34-4.inPlainWords: Cough syrups, decongestants and the antihistamine products in cold medicines have not been shown to work better than a placebo in children, and in a small child the risks are sedation, a racing heart from a decongestant, and an accidental overdose when two bottles contain the same ingredient. No such medicine should be given to an infant under two except on a doctor's instruction, and many paediatricians extend that to under six. What helps a blocked nose is saline drops, a humid room, fluids and time; what helps a fever is paracetamol or ibuprofen by weight.
34-4.benefit: A Cochrane review pooled 29 randomised trials, 10 of them in children. For every class of over-the-counter cough medicine, the paediatric trials found no benefit over placebo: cough suppressants, antihistamines, antihistamines with decongestants, and cough medicines with bronchodilators. Adverse events were reported in 21 of the studies, and the products containing an antihistamine or dextromethorphan had more of them. Indian labels for paediatric cold products are approved by CDSCO and carry an age band and a dose by age, and most say the product should not be used below a stated age except on medical advice. The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 require the label to declare every active ingredient and its quantity, so you can see whether the syrup duplicates paracetamol you are already giving.
34-4.cost: There is no cost at all, and you save the price of the bottle.
34-4.caveats: Check the whole panel, because many cold syrups contain paracetamol, and a second paracetamol dose on top of a fever dose is a real overdose risk. Honey beat placebo for a cough in one trial, but it must not be given before twelve months because of infant botulism. A cough in a small child that persists, or comes with fast breathing, a chest that pulls in, or a fever, is a reason to see a doctor rather than to change syrup. Do not use a left-over antibiotic for the same reason. The evidence grade is B because there are few trials for each class of medicine and the authors could not pool them into one figure.
34-4.sources: Smith SM, Schroeder K, Fahey T (2014). Over-the-counter (OTC) medications for acute cough in children and adults in community settings. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (11):CD001831. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD001831.pub5>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/opencms/en/Home/>

34-6.title: In India omeprazole needs a prescription: take it for a short course under a doctor, and act on the red flags
34-6.inPlainWords: Omeprazole and the other proton-pump inhibitors are Schedule H drugs in India, so a pharmacy may sell them only against a prescription from a registered medical practitioner, and the over-the-counter pack sold in some countries does not exist here. Used for a short course for heartburn that a doctor has assessed, it is safe for most people, but it is a treatment for a diagnosis rather than a permanent habit. Trouble swallowing, pain on swallowing, vomiting blood, black tarry stools, unexplained weight loss or anaemia are red flags: go to a doctor or an emergency department instead of taking an acid blocker, because the drug can mask a bleeding ulcer or a stomach cancer while it makes you feel better.
34-6.benefit: Omeprazole shuts down the acid pump in the stomach lining, which is why it works for reflux and for an ulcer, and why it also removes the warning signal of a cancer that is bleeding slowly. If the symptoms come back within a few weeks of stopping, the answer is an investigation, often an endoscopy or a test for H. pylori, not another course bought on your own. Omeprazole also reduces the effect of clopidogrel, so anyone with a stent or a recent heart attack must tell the cardiologist, who may switch to pantoprazole. Long courses are linked to low magnesium and vitamin B12, a higher risk of C. difficile infection and a slightly higher fracture risk, which is why a repeat prescription should be reviewed once a year.
34-6.cost: A consultation plus a generic omeprazole course costs little. The expensive part is ignoring a red flag for six months while the acid blocker keeps the symptom quiet.
34-6.caveats: The dose and the length of the course belong to the doctor: do not borrow a friend's strip or finish an old one. Over 55, with new or changing symptoms, the doctor will usually investigate before treating. Do not stop a long-standing prescribed PPI abruptly without asking, because the acid can rebound for a week or two. Antacids and alginates are the over-the-counter options for mild reflux, and they work for minutes rather than days. Tell the pharmacist about any other medicine you take, especially a blood thinner.
34-6.sources: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, Schedule H and the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. <https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/resources/UploadCDSCOWeb/2022/drug_rules/Drugs%20Rules1945n.pdf>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/opencms/en/Home/>; Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, pharmacovigilance. <https://ipc.nic.in/>

34-7.title: Do not ask for an antibiotic for a cold, and do not accept one without a prescription
34-7.inPlainWords: A cold is a viral infection, so an antibiotic does nothing for it: in the trials below it did not shorten the illness, and it made side effects about twice as likely. In India these drugs are Schedule H or H1, sold only against a prescription and, for the H1 group, written into the pharmacy's register, so a shop that sells you one across the counter is breaking the rule rather than doing you a favour. The exception is a bacterial complication that a doctor diagnoses on examination, such as an ear infection or pneumonia, which is a different decision.
34-7.benefit: A Cochrane review pooled six randomised trials with 1,147 participants and found no significant difference in cure or in persistent symptoms when an antibiotic was compared with placebo for a cold (RR 0.83, 95 per cent CI 0.60 to 1.14). The risk of an adverse reaction was 1.8 times higher overall (CI 1.01 to 3.21), and 2.62 times higher in adults (CI 1.32 to 5.18). For a purulent runny nose lasting under ten days there was no clear benefit either (RR 0.73, CI 0.47 to 1.13), with a 46 per cent higher risk of side effects. The authors concluded that routine antibiotics are not recommended for either condition, and the review is the 2025 update of a search that ran to 2013.
34-7.cost: It costs nothing and saves the price of the course. The larger saving is to the hospital patient who later needs a drug that still works.
34-7.caveats: Left-over antibiotics at home should not be used for a new illness: the drug may be the wrong one, the course incomplete and the expiry date past. A cold that lasts more than ten days, or worsens after seeming to improve, or comes with a high fever and breathlessness, needs a doctor. A child with ear discharge or a chest infection is one of the cases where an antibiotic is right, and that call is made after an examination. The evidence grade is B: the review shows that antibiotics do not help, and the benefit rating rests on avoiding their adverse effects rather than on preventing deaths.
34-7.sources: Kenealy T, Arroll B (2025). Antibiotics for the common cold and acute purulent rhinitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 11:CD000247. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000247.pub4>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, Schedule H and H1. <https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/resources/UploadCDSCOWeb/2022/drug_rules/Drugs%20Rules1945n.pdf>

34-10.title: Clear out expired and unused medicines once a year, and take them to a pharmacy or hospital collection point, not the kitchen bin
34-10.inPlainWords: Nearly half of the unsupervised medicine ingestions in young children involve prescription tablets, and about three in ten of those prescriptions belong to a grandparent, so the cabinet itself is the risk. Household medicines in India are not covered by the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, which bind hospitals and clinics, so there is no national kerbside collection: the practical route is a pharmacy or hospital that runs a take-back or a biomedical-waste collection point, and where none exists, whatever your municipal body says about household hazardous waste. Never flush them down the toilet or the drain, and never burn them.
34-10.benefit: U.S. emergency-department surveillance estimated that children under six took medicines without adult supervision about 640,000 times between 2004 and 2013, with about 59,000 visits in 2013 alone. From 2010 to 2013 the commonest form was an oral prescription tablet, 45.9 per cent of cases, and among prescriptions opioids (13.8 per cent) and benzodiazepines (12.7 per cent) led. A 2017 survey of five U.S. poison centres found that 30.7 per cent of prescription ingestions involved a grandparent's medicine, and that 51.5 per cent of the drugs had been taken out of their original packaging first. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration names take-back programmes as the best route, which is the same conclusion the Indian pharmacy route reaches.
34-10.cost: No cost. Sort the cabinet once a year, which takes about ten minutes.
34-10.caveats: Do not tip loose tablets into a bag with food waste, because a child or a stray animal can still reach them, and keep them in the original box until you hand them over so the collection point can read the label. Antibiotics should never be kept for next time, and neither should a half-used course of anything. Tablets decanted into a weekly organiser lose their label, so dispose of those rather than storing them. Local rules differ, so ask at the pharmacy counter first. The evidence grade is B because the U.S. figures are registry counts and no study measures how much a clean-out reduces ingestions.
34-10.sources: Lovegrove MC, Weidle NJ, Budnitz DS (2015). Trends in emergency department visits for unsupervised pediatric medication exposures, 2004-2013. Pediatrics, 136(4):e821-e829. <https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2015-2092>; Agarwal M, Lovegrove MC, Geller RJ, et al. (2020). Circumstances involved in unsupervised solid dose medication exposures among young children. Journal of Pediatrics, 219:188-195.e6. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpeds.2019.12.027>; U.S. Food and Drug Administration, where and how to dispose of unused medicines. <https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/where-and-how-dispose-unused-medicines>; Central Pollution Control Board, Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016. <https://cpcb.nic.in/>

34-11.title: No alcohol with metronidazole or a cephalosporin, and for several days after: the reaction is real and can be severe
34-11.inPlainWords: Metronidazole, tinidazole and several cephalosporins block the enzyme that clears alcohol, so a drink during treatment can bring flushing, sweating, a pounding heart, chest tightness, nausea and a fall in blood pressure, and in a bad case breathlessness and shock. The rule is no alcohol from the first dose until at least three days after the last one, and some labels say seven, because the enzyme takes days to recover. Alcohol is not only in a glass: many cough syrups, tonics and mouthwashes are made on an alcohol base, and some sweets and chocolates contain liqueur, so read the label and ask the pharmacist.
34-11.benefit: This is a disulfiram-like reaction: acetaldehyde builds up because the enzyme that should clear it is blocked. U.S. metronidazole labelling requires no alcohol during treatment and for at least three days afterwards, and no products containing propylene glycol. A hospital case series of 82 reactions found a cephalosporin in about 70 per cent of cases and metronidazole or tinidazole in about 12 per cent; the alcohol came from a drink in about half the cases and from an alcohol-containing medicine in about 38 per cent, and most patients recovered within one to three hours. Not every cephalosporin triggers it, and a patient cannot tell which one has been prescribed, so the rule covers all of them.
34-11.cost: No money at all. You abstain from alcohol for a little over a week and read the labels of the other medicines you take.
34-11.caveats: Tell the doctor if you have drunk in the last day or two when the prescription is written, and tell the pharmacist about any syrup you already use. If flushing, palpitations or breathlessness starts, stop drinking at once and get to a hospital if it does not settle within minutes. Do not drink with paracetamol either, and do not treat a course of antibiotics as a reason for a farewell drink. A single glass is enough to trigger it, so there is no safe amount during the window. The evidence grade is B because the evidence is case series and product labelling, not controlled trials.
34-11.sources: Metronidazole capsules, prescribing information, contraindications and interaction with alcohol. DailyMed, U.S. National Library of Medicine. <https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/>; Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, pharmacovigilance programme of India. <https://ipc.nic.in/>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/opencms/en/Home/>

34-12.title: Do not drive, work at heights or run machinery on a cold medicine containing chlorpheniramine or diphenhydramine
34-12.inPlainWords: The older antihistamines, chlorpheniramine and diphenhydramine, are in a large share of multi-symptom cold and allergy products, and they cause real drowsiness and slow reaction time, not just a feeling of tiredness. The warning on the label is not a formality: in the driving-simulator trial below, drivers on diphenhydramine did worse than drivers at a blood alcohol level of 0.10 per cent, and their own rating of how sleepy they felt did not predict it. Indian labels for these products carry the standard warning not to drive or operate machinery while taking them, and the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 require that warning to be printed.
34-12.benefit: The trial gave 40 drivers with allergic rhinitis four treatments in random order: diphenhydramine 50 mg, fexofenadine 60 mg, enough alcohol to reach a blood alcohol level of 0.10 per cent, and a placebo. Diphenhydramine produced the worst speed tracking and vehicle control, significantly worse than both alcohol and fexofenadine. When a vehicle pulled out unexpectedly, the drivers on alcohol or diphenhydramine reacted late, while fexofenadine was indistinguishable from placebo. The drivers' own ratings of drowsiness did not match their measured impairment. The newer antihistamines, loratadine, cetirizine and fexofenadine, cause far less sedation, so a pharmacist can usually swap the product rather than the plan.
34-12.cost: Free. Read the active ingredients before you buy, and take the bus or ask for a non-sedating alternative for the days you must drive.
34-12.caveats: Chlorpheniramine is often combined with paracetamol, so the same tablet can be a double-dose risk as well. Alcohol, some cough syrups and sleeping tablets add to the impairment, so the combination is worse than either alone. A driver impaired by a medicine can be prosecuted for rash or negligent driving, and section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 covers driving under the influence. Cetirizine still makes a minority of people sleepy, so test it on a day you are not driving. The evidence grade is B: the trial is small, but it is controlled and the result is consistent with the labelling.
34-12.sources: Weiler JM, Bloomfield JR, Woodworth GG, et al. (2000). Effects of fexofenadine, diphenhydramine, and alcohol on driving performance: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in the Iowa driving simulator. Annals of Internal Medicine, 132(5):354-363. <https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-132-5-200003070-00004>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/opencms/opencms/en/Home/>; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. <https://morth.gov.in/>
